concept.name: GARCH model
concept.definition: Generalized ARCH: a model in which the conditional variance depends on both past squared innovations and past conditional variances, parsimoniously capturing the slowly decaying volatility persistence of financial returns. Introduced by Bollerslev (1986).
concept.intuition: Variance today is a weighted average of a long-run level, yesterday's shock, and yesterday's variance estimate: a smoothing recursion that reacts to shocks but relaxes back to normal gradually.
concept.mechanics: GARCH(p,q) sets sigma_t^2 = omega + sum_{i=1}^q alpha_i epsilon_{t-i}^2 + sum_{j=1}^p beta_j sigma_{t-j}^2; a GARCH(1,1) approximates a high-order ARCH with three parameters and is estimated by (quasi-)maximum likelihood. Covariance stationarity requires the persistence sum alpha + beta to be below 1, though values near 1 are typical for daily asset returns.
concept.formula: sigma_t^2 = omega + alpha epsilon_{t-1}^2 + beta sigma_{t-1}^2 with omega > 0, alpha >= 0, beta >= 0, alpha + beta < 1; the unconditional variance is omega / (1 - alpha - beta).
concept.failure_modes: Symmetric GARCH misses the asymmetric response of volatility to negative shocks (addressed by EGARCH and GJR-GARCH), and structural breaks are absorbed as near-unit persistence. Quasi-MLE standard errors are fragile if the innovation distribution is misspecified.
concept.misconceptions: That a GARCH forecast of high volatility implies a predictable direction for returns: GARCH forecasts variance only and says nothing about the sign of returns.
concept.example: Fitting GARCH(1,1) to daily equity returns typically yields alpha around 0.08 and beta around 0.90, so a volatility shock decays with a half-life of roughly 6-7 trading days.
